item.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
item.description: null As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines." The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage. V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shared this chart depicting the evolution of SpaceX's Starship vehicles from the V2 to the planned V4 variant in August 2025. Exact specifications for Starship V4 are evolving. (Image credit: SpaceX/Elon Musk) Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9 , SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide. This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027. That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height." So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall. item.title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
item.description: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search . Read full article Comments

item.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
item.description: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. item.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
item.description: The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. Read full article Comments

item.title: Meet the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson
item.description: The Internet has been abuzz for months about which actor would replace Daniel Craig as British agent 007 James Bond in the franchise. We finally have the answer: Robert Pattinson , who built on his 2005 role as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire into an illustrious career mixing roles in franchises and Hollywood blockbusters with daring arthouse fare. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement . “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.” The choice will reunite Pattinson with Denis Villeneuve, who recently worked with him on the forthcoming Dune: Part III and will direct the next (as yet untitled) Bond installment. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement . We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.” Read full article Comments

item.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
item.description: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . item.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
item.description: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee!
item.description: Tems is officially a 12-time Grammy nominee after securing four nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards. Photo Credit: Tems/Instagram One, two, three… and now 12! Tems has added four more Grammy nominations to her record, bringing her career total to 12 ahead of the 69th Grammy Awards. The latest recognition also makes her the first Nigerian female artist to receive four nominations in a single Grammy year, with this year’s shortlist recognising her work across four categories. The Nigerian singer is in contention for Best Global Music Album with her 10-track EP, Love Is a Kingdom , and Best African Music Performance for “ Big Daddy ”. She has also earned nominations for Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “ What You Need ”. The four nominations give her one of the most extensive Nigerian representations at this year’s ceremony and bring her Grammy wins to two, following previous victories in 2023 and 2025. Her relationship with the Recording Academy began in 2022, when she received her first nomination for her contribution to Wizkid ‘s “ Essence ”, which was nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 64th Grammy Awards. The following year brought three more nominations, this time for her work on Future’s “ Wait for U ” featuring Drake and Beyoncé ‘s Renaissance . She won her first Grammy that night, taking home Best Melodic Rap Performance for “Wait for U”, while also receiving nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rap Song. Tems earned another nomination at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024 for “ Lift Me Up ”, her contribution to the Black Panther : Wakanda Forever soundtrack, in the Best Song Written for Visual Media category. She returned to the Grammys the following year with three nominations, including Best Global Music Album for her debut album, Born in the Wild , and Best R&B Song for “ Burning ”. Her second Grammy win came in the Best African Music Performance category, where “ Love Me JeJe ” took home the award at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025. Now, with four nominations for the 69th edition, Tems has added another significant chapter to her Grammy record. The ceremony will take place on Sunday, 7 February 2027, at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The post Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
item.description: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale. In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with en

What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
item.description: null After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA. Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year . Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space. For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement. By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth , a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. A NASA visualization showing Voyager 1 looking back towards the solar system as it approaches one light-day away from Earth. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe. Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977 . Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day. Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2 , which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035. item.title: ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
item.description: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg , the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

item.title: NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
item.description: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim , who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag , a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important , assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two tem

item.title: German Bundestag Lets Customs Freeze Crypto Over €100,000 Without a Criminal Case as the Bill Goes to the Bundesrat
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine German Bundestag Lets Customs Freeze Crypto Over €100,000 Without a Criminal Case as the Bill Goes to the Bundesrat The German Bundestag on Thursday approved a government bill that would let customs freeze cryptocurrency and other assets worth more than €100,000 when their lawful origin appears implausible, without first opening a criminal case. Permanent confiscation would still take a finance-court judgment. The measure still needs the Bundesrat’s consent before a planned Jan. 1, 2027 start, and the timing of that upper-house vote remains unclear. The Bundestag passed the Customs Financial Justice Act, a Finance Ministry overhaul to strengthen the customs administration and fight financial crime, on Nov. 12. The federal government introduced the bill on Sept. 30. The Finance Committee recommended passage on Nov. 11, with the Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and Alternative for Germany in favor, The Left opposed and the Greens abstaining. Crypto is covered but not singled out Crypto is covered expressly, using the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets definition, but it is not singled out. The same administrative procedure applies to cash, cars, real estate and other property. It reaches only “significant” assets: generally those worth more than €100,000, or more than €50,000 if the asset must be entered in a public register, such as vehicles or land. Because crypto is not registered that way, the €100,000 threshold applies. Customs may estimate the value, and closely related items can be treated as one asset. Customs offices — not Germany’s Financial Intelligence Unit, which the same bill strengthens separately — may freeze those assets for up to 30 days without a criminal case if there are factual indications the origin is not lawful, meaning lawful acquisition “does not appear plausible.” A finance court may extend that hold once by 150 days. That extension is decided by a single judge, without a hearing, in an order that cannot be appealed. Filing a confiscation application stops the clock until the court rules, so the often-cited 180-day period is not a hard cap. Permanent confiscation still requires a finance-court panel to be convinced the origin is unlawful. The committee shifted that decision away from a single judge. Owners must be told they are not required to produce records, and anything they do provide may be used in tax and criminal cases. The official justification says mere silence, or a denial of knowledge, will as a rule not be enough to prevent confiscation. Supporters and critics split Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said in August that if suspects cannot show assets were legally acquired, “the Porsche or the Rolex are gone for now.” In Thursday’s debate, Social Democrat Ingo Vogel told the Bundestag that criminally acquired assets do not enjoy constitutional property protection, and that the bill is “no automatic confiscation” and “no blanket reversal of the burden of proof.” The Bundesrat, in an e

item.title: Ubuntu gets AI-generated security fixes for those feeling brave
item.description: Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive , an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company . At the previous such event in June , the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism ). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022 , Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30 , surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS wor

item.title: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
item.description: null TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters. Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet. "This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said. Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1 , 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead. When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space. "We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained. Victor Glover speaking at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, 2026. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic/Future) The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center , toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station . But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home. Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard. "You should have this talk with our daughters." And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have. "We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard." The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life , by Chief Tecumseh. The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking. "It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for." After trav

item.title: Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage
item.description: Microsoft has released an out-of-band update to fix licensing and activation errors introduced by November's Windows security update. The fix is available from the Microsoft Update Catalog for Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019, Windows 10 22H2 ESU, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and 2019. Windows 11 23H2 users can obtain it from the Catalog or through Windows Update's Optional updates menu. The "non-security OOB update" targets affected enterprise devices. Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter). "This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing." Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said. Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release . Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage. Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July . On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 " permanently vulnerable ." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear. Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability." Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week. Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ®

item.title: Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
item.description: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X , referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. item.title: Aston Martin, Williams reveal special Las Vegas GP liveries
How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
item.description: Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct. I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek . I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece. Advertisement The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now , so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today. I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to cons

item.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
item.description: null The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space. The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society , another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034. Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars , along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your Leonid photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
item.description: Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania , one in New York , and one in Wisconsin . Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania's health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state's seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County , but state health officials have not confirmed it. For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they're the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania's case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650. Read full article Comments

item.title: Russia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
item.description: Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Grégoire Roos, Director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. As European countries prepare to take part in the next round of Ukraine peace talks, Roos questions whether having five European representatives could weaken their negotiating position. "The other option is to realize that it dilutes the negotiating power of Europe. And I would lean towards that," he says, proposing Finnish President Alexander Stubb as a possible representative. Roos also points to differences between Washington and European governments over negotiations with Russia. While "the Americans do absolutely want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine and Europe," he argues that European governments have little choice but to maintain pressure on Moscow, which has yet to abandon its "maximalist demands."

item.title: Davido, Tems & Ayra Starr Take 3 of 5 Best Global Music Album Spots at 2027 Grammys
item.description: Nigerian music stars Ayra Starr, Davido, and Tems claim three of the five slots in the Best Global Music Album category at the 69th Grammy Awards. The music industry in Nigeria is in a celebratory mood right now as three Nigerian artists — Davido , Tems , and Ayra Starr — are officially in the running for the prestigious Best Global Music Album award at the 69th Grammy Awards. Presented annually by the Recording Academy, the Best Global Music Album category honours full-length studio albums and extended plays that celebrate non-Western musical traditions and cross-cultural sounds from around the world. Claiming three out of the five available spots in a single year marks an extraordinary showing for Nigerian music on the international stage. Marking his sixth career Grammy nod, Davido is nominated for his sixth studio album, Oriadé . Released on 31 July 2026 to commemorate 15 years in the music industry, the 13-track project draws its title from the Yoruba words for destiny (“Ori”) and crown (“Adé”). Across songs featuring Black Sherif , Mayorkun , Fola , Leon Thomas , Aya Nakamura , and Llona , the album reflects on gratitude, ambition, and his musical roots across Afrobeats, R&B, and amapiano. This nod follows three nominations at the 66th Grammys in 2024 ( Timeless for Best Global Music Album, “ Feel ” for Best Global Music Performance, and “ Unavailable ” featuring Musa Keys for Best African Music Performance), a nomination in 2025 for “ Sensational ” alongside Chris Brown and Lojay , and a 2026 nod for “ With You ” featuring Omah Lay . Tems is also competing for the prize with her seven-track extended play, Love Is a Kingdom , which arrived as a surprise release on 21 November 2025. Built around alternative R&B and Afrobeats rhythms, the project explores romance, self-worth, and spiritual reflection across tracks including “ First “, “ Big Daddy “, “ Lagos Love “, and “ What You Need “. Beyond her album recognition, Tems leads the Nigerian contingent at the 69th Grammy Awards with four nominations in total, becoming the first Nigerian female artist to earn four nods in a single year. She is also nominated for Best African Music Performance for “Big Daddy”, as well as Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “What You Need”. A two-time Grammy winner, she previously claimed Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her contribution to Future’s “Wait for U” featuring Drake, and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “ Love Me JeJe “, while her debut album Born in the Wild was nominated in this global album category in 2025. Rounding out the Nigerian trio is Ayra Starr , who makes her debut appearance in the Best Global Music Album category with her third studio album, Starrgirl . Released on 14 August 2026, the 15-track album captures her growth and confidence across songs such as “ Tornado “, “ Heaven Baby ” featuring Zayn , “ Hot Body “, “ Who’s Dat Girl ” with Rema , and “ Gimme Dat ” with Wizkid . Ayra Starr picked up a second nom

item.title: US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
item.description: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration , signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times . "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. item.title: Harvard Holds 3.04 Million Bitcoin ETF Shares Steady
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Harvard Holds 3.04 Million Bitcoin ETF Shares Steady Harvard Management Company left its stake in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust unchanged at 3,044,612 shares in the third quarter, a position valued at $144.1 million as of Sept. 30 and now worth about $110.6 million after bitcoin’s slide. The university’s endowment manager disclosed the holding in a Form 13F filed Friday, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30. The share count is the same one Harvard reported on June 30 and on March 31. At 10:40 a.m. ET Monday, IBIT traded at $36.32, putting the stake at about $110.6 million, a paper decline of roughly $33.6 million, or 23%, from the value in the filing. The Sept. 30 close of $47.34 matches the price implied by the reported value. The same 3,044,612 shares were worth $101.4 million on June 30 and $117.0 million on March 31, so the position rose in value during the third quarter as bitcoin recovered, then gave back a large share of that gain after the quarter ended. Even after the November slide, the stake is still worth more than it was at midyear. IBIT was Harvard’s eighth-largest position among 18 holdings in a 13F portfolio valued at $3.95 billion, or about 3.6% of that publicly disclosed book of U.S. securities, which does not include the rest of the endowment. The largest holding was Space Exploration Technologies, reported at $1.29 billion. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing was second, at $616.5 million. That ranking is a sharp change from late 2025, when the bitcoin ETF was Harvard’s largest publicly disclosed position. First bought in 2025, then cut, then held Harvard first reported an IBIT position in its filing for the quarter ended June 30, 2025: 1,906,000 shares worth $116.7 million. It had not listed the fund in earlier 13Fs, including the report for March 31, 2025. By Sept. 30, 2025, Harvard had tripled the stake to 6,813,612 shares, valued at $442.9 million, making IBIT its largest public holding. The endowment trimmed that position by about 21% in the fourth quarter of 2025, to 5,353,612 shares worth $265.8 million, and opened a first stake in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust of 3,870,900 shares, valued at $86.8 million. It cut the bitcoin ETF again in the first quarter of 2026, by about 2.31 million shares, or 43%, to the 3,044,612 shares it still reported on Sept. 30, and sold the Ethereum fund entirely. The latest filing lists no other bitcoin or crypto ETFs. The remaining IBIT position is still larger, in share terms, than the 1.91 million shares Harvard first disclosed. Gold now outweighs the bitcoin ETF Harvard’s gold ETFs are now much larger than its bitcoin position. The same 13F lists 1,161,000 shares of SPDR Gold Shares worth $442.2 million, the portfolio’s third-largest holding, and 1,980,085 shares of the iShares Gold Trust worth $154.6 million. Combined, the two gold funds were valued at $596.8 million, more than four times the IBIT stake. The iShares Gold Trust share count was unchanged from June

item.title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
item.description: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase

item.title: Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state
item.description: Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids. The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University. But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information. Advertisement Read more SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says. The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington. This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants . The findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao , a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns. Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he says. “There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],”

item.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you." Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age. According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence. So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public? Odd detections at Colorado Springs Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs. At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth. item.title: Criminals attack French postal operator subsidiary, grab contact details of 22M people
item.description: The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say. La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste. Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September. The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend. Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data. However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently. In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year. On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year. item.title: Supreme Court Ends Custodia Bank’s Fight for a Fed Master Account, Leaving the Fed Free to Deny Crypto Banks Access
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Supreme Court Ends Custodia Bank’s Fight for a Fed Master Account, Leaving the Fed Free to Deny Crypto Banks Access The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank’s petition to review the Federal Reserve’s refusal to give the Wyoming bitcoin bank a master account, ending chief executive Caitlin Long’s years-long fight for direct access to the central bank’s payment rails. The case, Custodia Bank, Inc. v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, No. 26-62, is listed under “certiorari denied” on the Court’s Monday order list . The denial leaves in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that regional Federal Reserve Banks have discretion to reject even eligible applicants, and it closes the last court path Custodia had to force the Fed’s hand. A master account is a bank’s account at a Federal Reserve Bank, and the entry point to Fedwire and other payment services. Without one, a state-chartered bank has to rely on a correspondent institution to move money. Eligible, then turned away Custodia is a Wyoming special purpose depository institution, a charter that bars it from making loans and requires dollar deposits to be fully reserved in liquid assets. After receiving that charter, it applied for a master account at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in October 2020. In January 2021, the Kansas City Fed confirmed the bank was legally eligible and told it there were “no showstoppers.” In August 2021, Custodia also applied for Federal Reserve membership. While those requests sat pending, the Board of Governors in August 2022 published guidelines for evaluating master-account applications. The rules put firms that are neither federally insured nor supervised by a federal banking agency into “Tier 3,” the group that “generally receive[s] the strictest level of review.” Custodia fell into that bucket. On January 27, 2023, the Kansas City Fed denied the master account, citing an “unprecedented” business model “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities” and concluding the risks were “highly likely” to be “inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The same day, the Board denied Custodia’s membership application, saying approval “would be inconsistent with the financial, managerial, and corporate powers factors.” The last Custodia appeal fails Custodia had already sued the Fed and the Kansas City Fed in June 2022 over the delay. On March 29, 2024, U.S. District Judge Scott W. Skavdahl in Wyoming ruled that the Federal Reserve Act gives Reserve Banks discretion to grant or deny master accounts, dismissed Custodia’s Administrative Procedure Act claim for lack of a final agency action, and granted the Kansas City Fed summary judgment. The Tenth Circuit affirmed on October 31, 2025, in a 2-1 decision Bitcoin Magazine covered at the time. item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
item.description: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. item.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
item.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...
